info.title: Hidesay Bot API
info.summary: The HTTP API a bot uses to talk to a Hidesay server.
info.description:
This is the API a bot programme speaks. It lives under `/bot/v1` on the same server the app uses.

A bot is an account that a programme controls. A person makes it from the `@bot` console inside the app, gets a token, and from then on the programme does everything with that token. A bot has no session, no wallet, no calls and no devices: it has this API and nothing else.

**Envelope.** Every answer is JSON. A success is `{"ok": true, "result": ...}`. A failure is `{"ok": false, "error": {"status", "code", "message"}}` with the same status on the HTTP line. The `code` is stable and is what your programme should branch on; the `message` is for a person reading a log. A JSON body can be up to 256 KiB (`413 too_large` past that, `400 bad_request` when it isn't JSON), and a request whose body takes longer than 5 minutes to arrive is cut off with a plain `408`. Without a valid token every path answers `401`; with one, a path that doesn't exist answers `404 not_found`.

**Two kinds of body.** A chat is either *readable* or *end-to-end encrypted*, and the server tells you which (`mode` on a chat, `expected` on an error). In a readable chat you send and receive `text`. In an encrypted chat you send and receive `armored`: an ASCII-armoured OpenPGP message. A bot that has published a public key (`PUT /key`) is *protected*: its private chats become encrypted and people's phones seal every message to it. A bot without a key is *open*: its private chats are readable, the server passes the words along, and the app tells people so before they write. Groups follow the group: a group with open history is readable, any other group is encrypted.

**Updates.** What happens in chats reaches the bot as updates, each with a growing `updateId`. Fetch them with `GET /updates` (long polling) or have them posted to a webhook (`POST /webhook`). Either way delivery is in order and at least once: keep the last `updateId` you handled and ignore anything you have already seen. Updates older than 72 hours are dropped, and so are the oldest when more than 10 000 pile up unread. Nothing comes from other bots, the AI assistant or `@bot`. While the owner has the bot paused nothing is queued at all, so what happens meanwhile never arrives, and what was queued before waits, for polling and webhook alike, until the bot runs again.

**Limits.** 600 API calls a minute per bot and 1 200 a minute per address. Sending is 30 messages a second overall, 20 a minute into any one group and 1 a second into any one private chat, and edits count the same way in a window of their own. Pins, reactions, room settings and room pictures land on every phone in the room, so they have a window too: 30 a minute in any one chat. Uploads are 30 a minute, chat pictures included, each file up to `limits.uploadBytesMax` bytes. Past any of these you get `429` (`flood_wait`, `slow_mode` or `rate_limited`) with `retryAfter` in seconds and a `Retry-After` header. Honour it: the counter does not move while you are waiting. Resolving a handle has a window of its own, 60 a minute, where a name nobody holds counts as five. `GET /me` lists every number this server enforces, in `limits`.

**Files and pictures.** Every `url` in an answer (a file's, a sticker's, a chat's picture) is a path on the API host, such as `/media/3f2a…`: fetch it from there, with no token. `Range` requests work, so a big file can come in parts.

**Privacy, in one paragraph.** A bot only ever receives what was addressed to it. In a private chat that is everything the person writes. In a group or a channel it is a command (`/start`, `/start@yourbot`), a mention (`@yourbot` by any of the bot's handles, or the bot's name picked from the list), a reply to one of the bot's messages (a comment under its post counts), and the presses of its buttons - unless the room lets the bot read every message. That is the room's decision, never the bot's: it is off when an admin adds the bot, an admin turns it on or off from the app, every member sees it on the roster and above the keyboard, and the bot is told in `my_chat_member` (`readsAll`). In an encrypted room the sender's phone applies the rule and seals the message to the bot as well; the server cannot read the words and does not try. Whatever the bot can fetch later - its history, the message a reply quotes, the reactions - follows the same rule: only what it was handed.

**What a bot cannot do, on purpose.** Secret messages, payments, wallets, calls, devices or push (those are a person's), anybody's phone number unless they share it from the bot's Web-Bot themselves, join a chat by itself or add people to one (an administrator adds the bot, people come in through links), own a chat, decide what it reads in a room (the room does), read anything it wasn't handed (history from before it arrived included), inline mode, games, login buttons, reply keyboards, scheduled sends, or edit other people's messages (a channel's posts excepted, with the right to edit them). It cannot search for people either: a handle somebody typed resolves to an id, because that handle is already public, and there is no listing and nothing by phone number. Each of these is left out by decision: it would either give a program power over people it has no business having, or make the server read what it promises not to.

**Web-Bots.** A bot can also have a web page of its own that the app opens inside its private chat, and that knows who opened it from data the server signs. Setting one up, checking who opened it and every call the page can make are in the Web-Bots section.

**Ids.** People, bots, groups and channels have ids of eight random digits, and the character in front says what it is: `48213907` a person, `B48213907` a bot, `G48213907` a group, `C48213907` a channel. They are strings everywhere, letter included. A private chat goes by the person on the other side, so in a private message `chat.id` and `from.id` are the same. Until November 2026 ids were bare integers from a counter; every account and chat got a new one then, and an id saved before that points at nothing.

tags.description:
A bot can have a web page of its own, its **Web-Bot**, that the app opens inside the bot's private chat. The page runs in the phone's browser engine with a frame around it, and drives the frame through `window.Hidesay.WebBot`: buttons, popups, storage, the QR scanner, biometrics, position, motion sensors and more. Where the two overlap the names are the ones Telegram's Mini Apps use, so a page written for those ports with little work (see *Coming from Telegram* at the end).

This section is the whole of it: setting a Web-Bot up, opening it, knowing who opened it, and every call the page can make. The bot's server needs one operation from here, `GET /webbot/key`, to check who is on the page.

## Setting it up

The owner does it in the app: **@bot**, then the bot, then **Web-Bot**.

| setting | what it takes |
| --- | --- |
| address | the page, `https://`, up to 512 characters, on a host name: an IP address, `localhost`, a `.local` name, a name without a dot and `user:password@` are all refused |
| terms | what people accept before they open it the first time: text up to 4 000 characters, a link (`https`), or both. Changing them asks everybody again at their next opening |
| loading screen | a logo (JPEG, PNG or WebP, up to 2 MB), a background and an accent colour (`#rrggbb`), shown until the page is ready |
| on or off | off takes the key out of the chat, and the links say there is nothing to open |

A paused bot has no Web-Bot either. Removing the Web-Bot leaves its CloudStorage alone: what people saved is there again if it comes back. Deleting the bot deletes all of it.

## Opening it

- **From the bot's chat**, with the key next to the text box. `chatType` is `private`.
- **From a link**, anywhere: `https://hidesay.me/yourbot/app`. Add `?startapp=word` to hand the page a word, which it reads as `startParam`: 1 to 64 letters, digits, `_` and `-`. A word with anything else in it is dropped. `chatType` is `link`.

When the bot has terms, the person reads and accepts them the first time, and again after they change. Then the app loads the address exactly as it was set and adds nothing to it: what the page needs to know arrives through the SDK. The loading screen stays until the page calls `ready()`, or until 2.5 seconds after it finished loading if it never does.

The app puts the SDK into the page before any of the page's own scripts run, for the page's own origin (scheme, host and port of the address) and in the main frame only. An iframe, or a page on another origin, gets neither the SDK nor any data. Another page of the same origin loads inside the frame and gets the SDK and the same `initData` again; the frame keeps the buttons and colours the last page set until a page changes them. A link to another origin opens in the phone's browser, and only when the person tapped it: a redirect or a script that tries to leave just stops.

The same file is served at `/web-bot.js` on the API host (`https://api.hidesay.com/web-bot.js`) for a page that also has to work in an ordinary browser. There every call does nothing, callbacks answer as if the person said no, and `initData` is empty. Loading it inside the app does no harm.

The engine is the phone's own: on Android the system WebView, the Chromium the Play Store keeps up to date. Each account and bot has a profile of its own, so cookies and local storage are never shared with another bot, or with another account on the same phone. Third-party cookies, mixed content and `file:` addresses are off. The user agent ends with `Hidesay/<app version> WebBot/1.0`.

## Who opened it: initData

`Hidesay.WebBot.initData` is a string the Hidesay server signed when the page was opened: who opened it, from where, when, and for which bot. `Hidesay.WebBot.initDataUnsafe` is the same thing already parsed, good for showing a name. For anything that matters, send the string to your server and check it there before believing a word of it.

| field | what it is |
| --- | --- |
| `user` | who opened the page, as JSON: `id`, `firstName`, `lastName`, `username`, `languageCode`, `photoUrl`, `bannerUrl`, `allowsWriteToPm` |
| `chatType` | `private` from the bot's chat, `link` from a link |
| `startParam` | the `startapp` word of the link, when there was one |
| `authDate` | when the server signed it, in Unix seconds |
| `botId` | the bot it was signed for, `B48213907` |
| `signature` | Ed25519, base64url without padding |

`user.id` is the id the bot sees in its updates. A field of `user` with nothing in it is left out. `photoUrl` and `bannerUrl` are pictures (not clips) and are left out when the person has blocked the bot. `allowsWriteToPm` is true when the person and the bot already have a chat and nobody blocked anybody: the bot may write to them (`requestWriteAccess` asks for it). A newer server may add fields; they are signed like the rest.

To check it:

1. Read the string as a form-encoded query (`+` is a space) and take `signature` out.
2. Write `yourBotId:WebBotData`, then every other field as `key=value`, sorted by key, one per line, joined with `\n` and nothing after the last. `yourBotId` is your bot's own id from `GET /me`, so data signed for another bot never passes.
3. Check the Ed25519 signature of those bytes (UTF-8) with the key from `GET /webbot/key`: 32 bytes in base64url, the same for every bot and public. Fetch it once and keep it.
4. Refuse data older than you like, from `authDate`. Somebody who keeps the page open gets fresh data by opening it again.

In Node, with nothing to install:

```js
import { createPublicKey, verify } from "node:crypto";

// the key from GET /bot/v1/webbot/key, wrapped the way node wants it
const webBotKey = createPublicKey({
  key: Buffer.concat([Buffer.from("302a300506032b6570032100", "hex"), Buffer.from(WEB_BOT_KEY, "base64url")]),
  format: "der",
  type: "spki",
});

// the person behind initData, or null; botId is your bot's own
function whoOpened(initData, botId, maxAgeSeconds = 3600) {
  const { signature, ...signed } = Object.fromEntries(new URLSearchParams(initData));
  if (!signature) return null;
  const text = [`${botId}:WebBotData`, ...Object.keys(signed).sort().map((k) => `${k}=${signed[k]}`)].join("\n");
  if (!verify(null, Buffer.from(text, "utf8"), webBotKey, Buffer.from(signature, "base64url"))) return null;
  if (Date.now() / 1000 - Number(signed.authDate) > maxAgeSeconds) return null;
  return { ...signed, user: JSON.parse(signed.user) };
}
```

In Python, `hidesay_bot.validate_web_bot_data` does the same.

## The page's SDK

Everything below lives on `window.Hidesay.WebBot`. It is there before the page's first script runs; there is nothing to load and nothing to wait for.

Nothing returns a promise. A call that waits for something takes a callback, and most also fire an event (the list is at the end). `onEvent(name, handler)` and `offEvent(name, handler)` add and remove handlers; inside one, `this` is `Hidesay.WebBot`.

When something can't be done the callback gets `false` or `null`. Storage callbacks, and a few events, say why with one of these names:

| error | when |
| --- | --- |
| `UNSUPPORTED` | not inside the app, or not on this phone (no home screen shortcuts on an iPhone, no phone number on the account) |
| `USER_GESTURE_REQUIRED` | it needs a tap on the page first |
| `ACCESS_DENIED` | the person said no, now or before |
| `CANCELLED` | the person closed the question or the picker |
| `BUSY` | another question is open, too much at once, or the Web-Bot is in the dock |
| `INVALID_PARAMS` | something missing or out of shape |
| `KEY_INVALID`, `VALUE_TOO_LONG`, `QUOTA_EXCEEDED` | storage, see there |
| `NETWORK_ERROR`, `FAILED` | the app couldn't reach the server, or the server said no |

**A tap first.** What a timer must not be able to start waits for a tap of the person's on the page: a finger down and up in the same spot within 0.8 seconds, not a scroll. The tap counts for 2 seconds and the first thing it starts spends it, so one tap is one link, one download, one question. These need one: `openLink`, `openHidesayLink`, `readTextFromClipboard`, `requestWriteAccess` (until the person allowed it), `requestContact`, `shareToChat`, `downloadFile` and a download the page starts by itself, `addToHomeScreen`, both `openSettings`, `window.open`, and a popup after the third in 30 seconds. Without a tap nothing happens and the callback, if there is one, says no.

**Questions to the person.** Position, the clipboard, biometrics, the camera and the microphone are asked once per bot, and the answer, yes or no, is kept. The person can take any of them back from the frame's menu (**Permissions**); taking back the camera, the microphone or the position reloads the page. Writing first is asked until they say yes, the phone number every time, and every download is confirmed. The phone may also ask its own question the first time the app needs the camera or the position. One question at a time: another one meanwhile gets `BUSY`. A question turned down twice is not put again while the page stays open; the page gets its no straight away.

**The dock.** The person can put the Web-Bot away and carry on in the app: it waits in a dock at the bottom until they bring it back. Meanwhile `isActive` is false, motion sensors pause, and whatever would draw over the app or act for the person answers `BUSY` or does nothing: popups, the scanner, questions, the clipboard, sharing, downloads, links, haptics, biometrics and position. The page keeps running, and storage and its own network calls work.

**Limits.** The app reads up to 200 messages a second from a page, keeps up to 16 calls waiting for an answer at once (more get `BUSY`), and drops a single message over about 1.2 MB.

## Startup values

| property | what |
| --- | --- |
| `initData`, `initDataUnsafe` | who opened the page, see above |
| `version` | the SDK's version, `"1.0"`; `isVersionAtLeast("1.0")` compares |
| `platform` | `"android"` or `"ios"`, `"unknown"` outside the app |
| `devicePerformance` | `"low"`, `"average"` or `"high"`, a rough class from the phone's memory and cores |

## Theme, size and safe areas

`colorScheme` is `"light"` or `"dark"`. `themeParams` holds the person's colours right now as `#rrggbb`: `bg_color`, `secondary_bg_color`, `section_bg_color`, `header_bg_color`, `bottom_bar_bg_color`, `text_color`, `hint_color`, `subtitle_text_color`, `section_header_text_color`, `link_color`, `accent_text_color`, `button_color`, `button_text_color`, `section_separator_color` and `destructive_text_color`. `themeChanged` fires when the person changes theme. The app never darkens a page on its own: follow `colorScheme`.

The same values are CSS variables on `<html>`, so a page can follow the theme without a line of script: `--hs-theme-bg-color`, `--hs-theme-text-color` and so on (`_` becomes `-`), plus `--hs-viewport-height`, `--hs-viewport-stable-height`, `--hs-safe-area-inset-top`, `-bottom`, `-left`, `-right` and `--hs-content-safe-area-inset-top`, `-bottom`, `-left`, `-right`.

`viewportHeight` and `viewportStableHeight` are the height of the page's area in CSS pixels, between the frame's header and its bottom bar; `viewportChanged` fires with `{isStateStable}` when it changes. `isExpanded` is always true: the frame has one height.

`safeAreaInset` and `contentSafeAreaInset` (`{top, bottom, left, right}`, CSS pixels) matter in fullscreen: the first is the phone's own bars, the second the frame's chip in the top corner. Outside fullscreen both are zero. `safeAreaChanged` and `contentSafeAreaChanged` fire on a change.

`isActive` is false while the app is in the background or the Web-Bot is in the dock; `activated` and `deactivated` fire when that changes.

## The frame

| call | what it does |
| --- | --- |
| `ready()` | the page is ready: the loading screen goes |
| `close()` | closes the Web-Bot |
| `expand()` | nothing: the frame has one height. It is there so pages written for Telegram run as they are |
| `requestFullscreen()`, `exitFullscreen()`, `isFullscreen` | fullscreen hides the header and leaves the frame's menu and dock buttons in a small chip in the top right corner (see the safe areas). `fullscreenChanged` fires on a change, `fullscreenFailed` with `{error: "ALREADY_FULLSCREEN"}` |
| `setHeaderColor(c)`, `setBackgroundColor(c)`, `setBottomBarColor(c)` | the header, the area behind the page and the bar under it: `#rrggbb`, or `bg_color`, `secondary_bg_color` or `bottom_bar_bg_color` to follow the theme. Anything else is ignored. `headerColor`, `backgroundColor` and `bottomBarColor` read them back, always as `#rrggbb` |
| `enableClosingConfirmation()`, `disableClosingConfirmation()`, `isClosingConfirmationEnabled` | when on, closing the page (the X, the back gesture, the menu) asks the person first |
| `enableVerticalSwipes()`, `disableVerticalSwipes()`, `isVerticalSwipesEnabled` | dragging the header down puts the Web-Bot in the dock; on unless the page turns it off |

The frame's menu always has Reload, Share (the Web-Bot's link), Add to home screen (Android), Permissions, the terms when there are some, and Close, whatever the page does: the person always has a way out.

**BackButton and SettingsButton.** `BackButton.show()` turns the X in the header into a back arrow, and from then on the arrow and the phone's back gesture fire `backButtonClicked` instead of closing; `hide()` gives the X back. `SettingsButton.show()` adds **Settings** to the frame's menu, and choosing it fires `settingsButtonClicked`. Both have `show()`, `hide()`, `isVisible`, `onClick(handler)` and `offClick(handler)`.

**MainButton and SecondaryButton.** Two buttons in a bar under the page, hidden until shown.

- `setText(text)`: up to 64 characters. With no text the app shows a generic one in the person's language.
- `show()`, `hide()`, `enable()`, `disable()`, `onClick(handler)`, `offClick(handler)`.
- `showProgress(leaveActive)` puts a spinner on it and disables it unless `leaveActive`; `hideProgress()` takes the spinner off and enables it again.
- `setParams({text, color, text_color, is_visible, is_active, has_shine_effect, position})` sets several at once. Colours are `#rrggbb` only.
- `text`, `color`, `textColor`, `isVisible`, `isActive`, `hasShineEffect` and `position` can be read and set; `isProgressVisible` only read.
- `SecondaryButton.position` is where it sits next to the main one: `left` (the default), `right`, `top` or `bottom`.
- Changes made one after the other reach the app together, on the next tick. A press fires `mainButtonClicked` or `secondaryButtonClicked`.

## Popups

`showPopup({title, message, buttons}, callback)` shows a box in the app's own style.

- `message` 1 to 256 characters, `title` up to 64, up to 3 `buttons`, each `{id, type, text}`.
- `type` is `default`, `ok`, `close`, `cancel` or `destructive`. `text` is up to 64 characters, and needed for `default` and `destructive`: the others say what the app says. `id` is up to 64 characters, the button's index (`"0"`, `"1"`, `"2"`) when left out. With no buttons there is one that closes.
- The callback gets the `id` of the button pressed, or `null` when the person dismissed the box or the frame didn't show it. `popupClosed` fires with `{button_id}`.
- Wrong parameters throw `Error("WebBotPopupParamInvalid")`; calling it while one is open throws `Error("WebBotPopupOpened")`.

`showAlert(message, callback)` and `showConfirm(message, callback)` are the two usual shapes; the second calls back with `true` for OK.

A page in a loop meets some brakes: one popup at a time, the next at least 0.4 seconds after the last one closed, and from the fourth in 30 seconds on only right after a tap. The page's own `alert()` and `confirm()` go through the same box and the same brakes; held back, `alert()` just returns and `confirm()` says no. `prompt()` always returns `null`, and the browser's "leave this page?" is never shown: use closing confirmation.

## Links

- `openLink(url)`: an `http` or `https` address opens in the phone's browser, outside the app. A Hidesay link (`https://hidesay.me/...` or `hidesay://...`) opens in the app instead, and the Web-Bot goes to the dock. Anything else (`tel:`, `mailto:`, `intent:`) is ignored. Needs a tap.
- `openHidesayLink(url)`: Hidesay links only, the same way. Another bot's Web-Bot, a chat, a post.
- Links and forms in the page: the same origin stays in the frame, anything else goes out as with `openLink`, and only on a tap. `window.open()` works from a tap and goes the same way.

## QR scanner

`showScanQrPopup({text}, callback)` opens the app's own scanner over the page, with `text` (up to 64 characters) under the camera; the page never sees the camera. Each code read reaches the callback and `qrTextReceived` (`{data}`, up to 4 096 characters). A code is reported once, and again only after it has been out of view for 3 seconds. Return `true` from the callback to close the scanner, or call `closeScanQrPopup()`; `scanQrPopupClosed` fires when it closes, whoever closed it. One scanner at a time. The phone asks for the camera the first time.

## Clipboard

`readTextFromClipboard(callback)` gives the text on the clipboard, up to 16 384 characters, or `null`. It needs a tap and asks the person the first time. `clipboardTextReceived` fires with `{data}`.

## Writing first and the phone number

`requestWriteAccess(callback)`: a bot writes only to people who have a chat with it. This asks the person to let the bot write first. On yes the chat is made, the bot receives `web_bot_write_access` (once per person, ever), and the callback gets `true`. Once allowed, later calls answer `true` without asking. Needs a tap the first time. `writeAccessRequested` fires with `{status}`, `"allowed"` or `"cancelled"`.

`requestContact(callback)` asks the person to share their phone number, every time. The number is the one verified on their account, never one typed. On yes the bot receives `web_bot_contact` and the callback gets `true` and `{responseUnsafe: {contact: {phone, firstName, lastName, userId}}}`: believe the update the bot received, not the page. An account with no number answers `false`. Needs a tap. `contactRequested` fires with `{status}`, `"sent"` or `"cancelled"`.

Both answer `false` when the person has blocked the bot, and the two together go through 30 times an hour at most.

## Sharing and downloads

`shareToChat(text, callback)`: the person picks one of their chats and `text` (1 to 4 096 characters) goes there as their own message. Needs a tap. The callback gets `true` once it is sent; `shareToChatSent` fires, or `shareToChatFailed` with `{error}`.

`downloadFile({url, file_name}, callback)`: `https` only. The person sees the file name and the site and confirms, and the file goes to the phone's downloads. The name loses any folder and odd character and stops at 128 characters; without one it is the last part of the address. Needs a tap. The callback gets `true` when the download started; `fileDownloadRequested` fires with `{status}`, `"downloading"` or `"cancelled"`. A download the page starts by itself, a link with `download` or an answer that is an attachment, goes through the same question.

## Home screen

`addToHomeScreen()` asks the launcher for a shortcut that opens the Web-Bot straight away (its `https://hidesay.me/yourbot/app` link), with the logo of the loading screen or the bot's picture. Android only: on an iPhone `homeScreenFailed` fires with `{error: "UNSUPPORTED"}`. Needs a tap. `homeScreenAdded` fires once the launcher really added it, which is never if the person says no there. `checkHomeScreenStatus(callback)` answers `"added"`, `"missed"`, `"unsupported"` or `"unknown"` and fires `homeScreenChecked` with `{status}`. The frame's menu has the same entry.

## Haptics

`HapticFeedback.impactOccurred(style)` with `light`, `medium`, `heavy`, `rigid` or `soft`; `HapticFeedback.notificationOccurred(type)` with `error`, `success` or `warning`; `HapticFeedback.selectionChanged()`. Each returns `HapticFeedback`, so they chain. Nothing happens when the person turned vibration off in the app, from the dock, or within 25 milliseconds of the last one.

## Storage

Three stores, each the bot's own and per person: one bot never reads another's, and two accounts on the same phone have their own.

| | CloudStorage | DeviceStorage | SecureStorage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| where | on the Hidesay server, the same on all the person's phones | on this phone | on this phone, sealed with the system keystore (Android Keystore, iOS Keychain) |
| keys | 1 to 128 of `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `_`, `-` | 1 to 128 characters, any | 1 to 128 of `A-Z`, `a-z`, `0-9`, `_`, `-` |
| a value | up to 4 096 characters | up to 1 048 576 characters | up to 2 048 characters |
| in all | 1 000 keys | 10 MiB of keys and values | 20 items |
| calls | `setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem`, `getItems`, `removeItems`, `getKeys` | `setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem`, `clear` | `setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem`, `clear` |

- Every callback is `callback(error, value)`. `setItem`, `removeItem`, `removeItems` and `clear` give `true`; `getItem` the value or `null`; `getItems(keys)` an object of key to value or `null`; `getKeys` every key, in alphabetical order. `getItems` and `removeItems` take up to 100 keys a call.
- Errors: `KEY_INVALID`, `VALUE_TOO_LONG`, `QUOTA_EXCEEDED` when it is full, and for CloudStorage `BUSY` (over 240 calls a minute), `NETWORK_ERROR` and `FAILED`.
- CloudStorage is not end-to-end encrypted: the server keeps it sealed on its disk but can read it. Secrets go in SecureStorage. A person's CloudStorage goes when they delete their account; DeviceStorage and SecureStorage go when the account leaves the phone.

## Biometrics

`BiometricManager` asks the phone to check that its owner is holding it, with the phone's own prompt.

- `init(callback)` comes first. It fills `isInited`, `isBiometricAvailable`, `biometricType` (`"finger"`, `"face"` or `"unknown"`), `isAccessRequested`, `isAccessGranted`, `isBiometricTokenSaved` and `deviceId`, random and fixed for this bot on this phone, saying nothing about the phone. `biometricManagerUpdated` fires.
- `requestAccess({reason}, callback)` asks the person, once, whether the bot may use it; `reason` (up to 128 characters) goes in the question. The callback gets `true` when it may.
- `authenticate({reason}, callback)` shows the prompt. On success the callback gets `true` and the token saved with `updateBiometricToken`, or `""` when there is none. `biometricAuthRequested` fires with `{isAuthenticated, biometricToken}`.
- `updateBiometricToken(token, callback)` keeps `token` (up to 1 024 characters) on the phone, sealed like SecureStorage but apart from its 20 items. Saving one shows the prompt first, so a page cannot swap it quietly; `""` removes it. `biometricTokenUpdated` fires with `{isUpdated}`.
- `openSettings()` opens the Web-Bot's permissions, after a tap.

What it proves, and what it doesn't:

- The prompt takes the fingerprint, the face **or the phone's PIN, pattern or password**, and the page isn't told which. `isBiometricAvailable` is true when the phone has any of them set up.
- It all happens on the phone; the Hidesay server sees none of it. For your server to rely on it, save a random secret with `updateBiometricToken`, keep it (or its hash) on your server next to the person's `user.id`, and have the page send it after `authenticate` hands it back.
- `biometricType` is the sensor the phone has; an Android phone with both says `"finger"`.
- Taking the permission back in the frame's menu deletes the token.

## Position

- `LocationManager.init(callback)` fills `isInited`, `isLocationAvailable`, `isAccessRequested` and `isAccessGranted`; `locationManagerUpdated` fires.
- `LocationManager.getLocation(callback)` asks the person the first time, then gives `{latitude, longitude, altitude, course, speed, horizontal_accuracy, vertical_accuracy, course_accuracy, speed_accuracy}` in degrees, metres and metres a second, `null` where the phone doesn't know. A fix from the last minute is used as it is; otherwise the phone has 15 seconds to find one. The callback gets `null` when the person said no or there was no fix. `locationRequested` fires with `{locationData}`.
- `LocationManager.openSettings()` opens the Web-Bot's permissions, after a tap.
- The page's own `navigator.geolocation` works too, under the same permission.

## Motion

`Accelerometer` gives `x`, `y` and `z` in m/s², gravity included; `Gyroscope` gives `x`, `y` and `z` in rad/s; `DeviceOrientation` gives `alpha`, `beta` and `gamma` in radians, and `absolute`. Each has:

- `start({refresh_rate, need_absolute}, callback)`: `refresh_rate` in milliseconds, 20 to 1 000, 1 000 when left out. `need_absolute`, for `DeviceOrientation`, asks for angles against magnetic north when the phone can give them, and `absolute` says whether it did. The callback gets `true` once it runs.
- `stop(callback)`, `isStarted`, and the last reading as properties.
- Events: `accelerometerStarted`, `accelerometerChanged`, `accelerometerStopped`, `accelerometerFailed` with `{error}`, and the same for `gyroscope` and `deviceOrientation`.

Nobody is asked. Readings pause while the app is in the background or the Web-Bot is in the dock and start again after; closing the Web-Bot stops them.

## Camera, microphone and files

`getUserMedia` works: the person is asked once per bot, and the answer for the camera and the one for the microphone are kept apart. `<input type="file">` opens the phone's own picker. Sound and video wait for a tap before they play.

- The object is `window.Hidesay.WebBot`. There is no `window.Telegram` to fall back on.

get.description:
Returns the updates waiting for the bot, oldest first, up to `limit`. With `timeout` the call hangs until something arrives or the clock runs out, and answers an empty list on the clock.

`offset` confirms: every update with an `updateId` below it is deleted and never shown again. Send the highest `updateId` you handled plus one. Without `offset` you get everything still in the queue, which is what a bot asks on its very first call.

Only one poll per bot at a time. A second call ends the first one at once with an empty answer, so two copies of the same programme polling one bot will starve each other: run one.

Not available while a webhook is set: delete the webhook first.

post.description:
From now on every update is POSTed as JSON to `url`, one update per request, in order, with the header `User-Agent: Hidesay-Bot-Api/1`. If you give a `secret`, every delivery carries it in the header `X-Hidesay-Bot-Api-Secret-Token`: check it and refuse anything without it.

Answer with any 2xx within 10 seconds and the update is considered delivered. Anything else, a timeout or a redirect counts as a failure: the server backs off (one second, then doubling, up to an hour) and tries that same update again, so delivery is at least once and never out of order. After ten failures in a row the owner is told in the app. Updates still queue while the webhook is failing and are kept for 72 hours.

The URL must be `https`, carry no credentials or fragment, and resolve to a public address. Setting a webhook ends any poll in progress; `GET /updates` refuses while one is set.

Deliveries arrive from addresses that change over time, so don't allow or block them by IP: check the secret token instead.

There is no way to remove the key from the API on purpose: downgrading a bot from protected to open is a decision for its owner, in the console.

The whole list of that scope, replaced. Up to 100 commands; a command is 1 to 32 lowercase letters, digits and underscores (a leading slash is dropped), its description 1 to 256 characters. Duplicates are folded to the first.

Scopes resolve the way Telegram's do, narrowest first: in a private chat `private` then `default`; in a group `chat:G48213907` (its own id), then `groupAdmins` for administrators, then `groups`, then `default`. post.description:
Into a chat the bot is in. Send `text` into a readable chat and `armored` into an encrypted one; the wrong kind is refused with `wrong_body_kind` and `expected` says which. Into a readable chat you can also send files (`media`, uploaded first with `POST /attachments`, `text` being the caption) or a `sticker`; into an encrypted one the files go up sealed and the envelope that points at them goes inside `armored`. In a group `media` needs the members' permission to send files, a voice note (`audio`) the one to send voice notes. `mentions` tags people the way the app does. A `markup` adds rows of buttons under the message. `replyTo` quotes a message of the same chat (a wrong id is silently dropped). `silent` only matters in a channel: the post goes out without a notification.

`sendId` makes the call safe to repeat: a UUID of your choosing, and a second call with the same one hands back the message already written instead of writing it twice. Use it whenever you retry after a timeout.

In an encrypted chat, seal the message to every key `GET /chats/{id}/keys` returns and to the bot's own key, sign it with the bot's key, and send the armoured result.

parameters.description: A person's or a bot's id. A person's also works as the bare digits.

delete.description: The *ban users* right. They can come back through a link; nobody is put back in.

lifted.description: False when there was no ban.

get.description: An admin with the *invite links* right sees every link. A member the group lets add people (and an admin without that right, in such a group) sees only the links the bot made itself.

post.description: Same right as listing them. A public chat already has its link, its name (`chat_is_public`). With `needsApproval` whoever uses it asks first, and the bots that may let people in get a `join_request`.

expiresAt.description: Unix milliseconds. Null or left out: it never expires.

maxUses.description: Null or left out: no limit.

get.description: The *add members* right.

parameters.name: userId
parameters.description: A person's or a bot's id. A person's also works as the bare digits.

post.description: Only somebody who asked (`request_not_found` otherwise): this is never a way round a person's "don't add me to groups". The *add members* right.

409.description: `chat_full`: the room has no seat left (a group holds 150 people, a channel 200).

patch.description: Comments on or off, whether the desk may sign its comments (left out: no), whether people who aren't subscribed may comment on a public readable channel (left out: as it was). The *manage comments* right. Answers the chat.

parameters.name: postId
parameters.description: A post of the channel, one the bot was handed.

patch.summary: Close or open one post's comments
patch.description: Whatever the channel as a whole says. The *manage comments* right.

get.description: For its admins: subscribers coming and going over 30 days, views per post, the best posts by id. No words: a bot that wasn't handed a post doesn't read it from here. `growth` is one bucket a day over 30 days, `windows` the last 7 and 30 days, the views add up over the last 100 posts, and `topPosts` is the best 10.

parameters.name: username
parameters.description: A public handle, without the `@`. 3-32 characters: letters, digits and underscore. Case does not matter.

get.summary: A public handle, turned into an id
get.description:
For the handle a person types at your bot - "paga @anna", "segui @notizie" - when no message has handed you that id. People, groups and channels share one pool of names, so a handle is held by exactly one of the three and `kind` says which.

The answer carries `id` at the top, and the same thing again under `user` or `chat` with what little goes with it. `username` is the name that account or chat actually goes by, which is not always the one you asked with: a person can answer to several handles.

It finds anybody with a public handle, which is no more than the short link already tells a stranger with a browser (`hidesay.me/anna`). The id on its own grants nothing: sending still needs the bot to be in the chat, and a key still needs somebody the bot may look up. Out of reach: a chat with no public name (a private group is not in the pool at all), an account that has been closed, and the server's own service account.

Harder limit than the rest of the API: 60 a minute, and a handle nobody holds counts as five, so about a dozen blind guesses spend the minute. Over it you get `429 flood_wait` with `retryAfter`.

200.description: What the handle turned out to be.

404.description: `username_not_found`: nobody and no chat answers to that name.

parameters.name: userId
parameters.description: A person's or a bot's id. A person's also works as the bare digits.

get.description: Only for somebody the bot may look up, by the same rule as `GET /users/{userId}`; anybody else is `user_not_found`, whether or not they exist.

post.description: For a programme that notices its token leaked. Nothing works again, this call included, until the owner issues a new token in the console; the owner is told at once. Works while paused.

get.summary: The key initData is signed with
get.description:
The public half of the key the server signs every Web-Bot's `initData` with: 32 raw bytes, base64url without padding. It is the same for every bot and needs no token, so fetch it once and keep it in your configuration. Cached for an hour; 120 calls a minute per address.

How to check `initData` with it is under *Who opened it: initData* above, with a Node example; the Python library does it in `validate_web_bot_data`.

post.summary: An update, delivered to your webhook
post.description: One update per request, in order. Answer any 2xx within 10 seconds. The header `X-Hidesay-Bot-Api-Secret-Token` carries the secret you set, if any; `User-Agent` is `Hidesay-Bot-Api/1`. Deliveries are at least once: a slow 2xx can be retried, so treat `updateId` as the thing that makes a delivery new. They come from addresses that change over time: trust the secret token, not the IP.

200.description: Any 2xx: delivered. Anything else, a timeout or a redirect: retried later.

botToken.description: The token the console showed once: `Authorization: Bearer pgpbot_41205736.<43 characters>`. The server keeps only a hash of it. A wrong, revoked or rotated token answers `401 unauthorized`. Keep it in an environment variable or a secrets store, never in a repository or a chat; if it leaks, rotate it from the console or burn it with `POST /token/revoke`.

chatId.name: chatId
chatId.description: A chat the bot is in: `G…` a group, `C…` a channel, a person's id for the private chat with them. Any other id answers `chat_not_found`.

error.message: missing, revoked or invalid bot token

Paused.description: `bot_paused`: the owner paused the bot. Only `GET /me`, `GET /webhook`, `DELETE /webhook` and `POST /token/revoke` work meanwhile.

BadRequest.description: `bad_request`: the body or the query is wrong; `message` says which field.

ChatNotFound.description: `chat_not_found`: no such chat, or the bot is not in it.

FloodWait.description: `flood_wait` (too many of these in their window), `slow_mode` (a send into a group in slow mode) or `rate_limited` (too many calls). Wait `retryAfter` seconds.

error.message: too many changes in this chat, wait 4s

message.description: For a person reading a log. Do not parse it.

expected.description: The body this chat takes. On `wrong_body_kind`, and on a `bad_request` for a send with neither `text` nor `armored`.

ErrorCode.description: Every code the API can answer with.

UserId.description: A person (`48213907`) or a bot (`B48213907`): eight random digits, never handed out twice, with a B in front for a bot.

ChatId.description: `G48213907` a group, `C48213907` a channel, `48213907` the private chat with that person. A private chat has no id of its own: it goes by the person on the other side.

ChatIdIn.description: A chat id as a string, letter included. The private chat with a person also takes their id as a bare number.

oneOf.description: A person's id: the private chat with them.

Self.description: The bot as it sees itself. No owner and no token are ever included.

id.description: The bot's own id: B and eight digits.

usernames.description: The other handles the owner added, oldest first. Each one reaches the bot exactly like the main one: in a link, in a mention, after the `@` of a command.

about.description: The bio under the name on the profile: up to `limits.aboutMax` characters, line breaks allowed.

description.description: What the bot does, shown before the first message.

queued.description: Updates waiting to be fetched or delivered.

Mode.description: `protected`: end-to-end encrypted, bodies are `armored`. `open`: readable, bodies are `text`.

lastOkAt.description: Unix milliseconds of the last successful delivery.

nextAttemptAt.description: Unix milliseconds of the next try while backing off.

Scope.description: `default`, `private`, `groups`, `groupAdmins`, or `chat:<id>` for one group or channel the bot is in (`chat:G48213907`). Missing means `default`.

command.description: Without the slash. The server trims it, drops a leading `/` and lowercases it before it checks, so `/Start` is taken as `start`.

description.description: Runs of spaces are made one.

InlineKeyboard.description: Rows of buttons under a message. Up to 20 rows, 8 buttons a row, 100 in all, 8 KiB of JSON. The buttons are not encrypted: the server has to know which one was pressed.

callbackData.description: Up to 64 bytes, no control characters, unique within the keyboard. Comes back in `callback_query`.

url.description: Absolute http(s) URL without credentials. The phone shows it before opening.

text.description: Readable chats. No control characters apart from newline and tab.

armored.description: Encrypted chats. An ASCII-armoured OpenPGP message.

markup.description: Null is the same as leaving it out.

sendId.description: Your id for this send, so a retry writes nothing twice.

media.description: Readable chats: files uploaded with `POST /attachments`, `text` as the caption. One file, or an album of 2 to 10 pictures and videos.

sticker.description: Readable chats: a sticker, see `GET /stickers/{id}`. No text with it. From a public pack, or one the bot was shown, with its `mediaId` as proof. In a group it counts as media: the members need the right to send media.

oneOf.description: A person's id as a bare number.

mentions.description: Groups: who the words tag (`@[Name](u48213907)`), so they are told even with the group muted, as for a person's tag. Somebody not in the group is dropped.

markup.description: Omit to keep the buttons, `null` to remove them.

SentMessage.description: A message of the bot's own, as a send, a forward, a comment or an edit hands it back. For a file, an album, a sticker or a forward in a readable chat, `text` is the body as the phones read it: the app's own format, a marker character and then JSON. Updates carry the bot's own messages only as the message a reply quotes (`replyToMessage`).

threadRoot.description: A comment: the post it hangs under.

UserRef.description: As much as a bot may know about a person: id, handle, name. Never a phone number.

Media.description: A file in a readable chat: a picture, a clip, a voice note (`audio`) or any other file. Fetch it from `url` on the same server; `plain` false means the blob is OpenPGP, sealed for the chat it was first sent to.

url.description: A path on the API host, `/media/<id>`: fetch it from there with no token. `Range` works.

sha256.description: Of the file as it opens, when the sender gave it. Check it after downloading.

Message.description: A message a person wrote, as a bot receives it. Either `armored` (encrypted chat: decrypt it with the bot's private key; inside is the same text or envelope) or `text` with `media`, `sticker`, `forward` and `link` (readable chat). A comment under a channel post has `threadRoot`.

from.description: Who wrote it. Null for a channel post that speaks as the channel, which is how subscribers see it too: the bot is never told who is behind an unsigned post.

signature.description: Channel posts with no `from` only: the name a signed post shows readers, or null when the channel does not sign its posts.

replyTo.description: The id of the message this one answers, when the bot was handed that one too. Null otherwise, even for a reply: the id alone would say which messages exist.

replyToMessage.description: The message `replyTo` quotes, when the bot was handed it too: its own, or one the room delivered to it. Null whenever `replyTo` is.

threadRoot.description: A comment: the channel post it hangs under.

kind.description: `user` for anything a person typed or attached.

markup.description: The buttons under it: only ever on a bot's message, as in a quoted one.

text.description: The words, or the caption of a file or an album. Formatting is the app's: `**bold**`, `__italic__`, `~~strike~~`, `||spoiler||`, `` `code` ``, ``` fenced blocks, `>` quote lines, `@handle`, and `@[Name](u48213907)` for a name picked from the list.

Seat.description: A membership, the bot's own or somebody's. `admin` carries the rights it holds; `member` and `restricted` carry what it may do; `left` and `kicked` carry nothing. A bot's seat also says whether the room lets it read everything (`readsAll`). The owner shows as `admin` with every right in `can`: read `can`, not `adminRights`, whose bits are the app's own.

can.description: Admins: each right of the badge, by name.

permissions.description: What this seat may do as a member, by name. All true for an admin.

readsAll.description: Bots only: the room lets this bot read every message, not only what is meant for it. Off when a bot comes in; the room's admins decide.

user.description: Private chats: the person, as `id`, `username`, `firstName`, `lastName`, `deleted` and `hasKey` (no `isBot`).

blocked.description: Private chats: they blocked the bot.

permissions.description: What an ordinary member may do here.

protectContent.description: Messages here can't be forwarded, copied or saved.

pinnedMessageIds.description: The pinned messages the bot could open: its own and the ones handed to it. A pin it never saw is left out.

me.description: Groups and channels: the bot's own seat. Not in the `chat` of an update.

allOf.description: A public group or channel seen from outside, which is as much as its short-link page shows. No `mode` and no seat: the bot is not in it.

historyVisible.description: Whether somebody walking in can read what was said before.

Resolved.description: What a handle turned out to be. Exactly one of `user` and `chat` is filled in; `kind` says which, and `id` is there either way so a caller that only wants the number never has to look.

id.description: The person's or bot's id, or the group's (`G…`) or channel's (`C…`).

username.description: The handle it actually goes by. A person who answers to several returns their main one, not the one you asked with.

user.description: Set when `kind` is `user`, with `hasKey` alongside. Null otherwise.

chat.description: Set when `kind` is `group` or `channel`. Null otherwise.

Update.description: One thing that happened. `kind` says which of the other fields is set.

updateId.description: Grows by one per update, per bot.

chat.description: Where it happened. `my_chat_member` and `chat_updated` carry the whole room for a group or channel (a `Chat`, as `GET /chats/{id}` has it, without `me`); a private one is always the short reference. Null only in a `web_bot_contact` from somebody who has no chat with the bot yet.

threadRoot.description: `message_reaction`: the post, when the message is a comment.

reactions.description: `message_reaction`: every reaction on the message now, by emoji.

changed.description: `chat_updated`: the settings that moved, by their `PATCH /chats/{id}` names, or `photo`, `banner`, `pinnedMessageIds`, `commentsEnabled`, `commentSigning`. A person changing the room in the app can also move `historyVisible`, `publicUsername`, `categories`, `lang` and `discoverHidden`.

from.description: Who did it. Null where the bot may not know: in a channel that hides its admins from a bot that isn't one, and in `my_chat_member` when the chat itself was deleted.

old.description: `my_chat_member` and `chat_member`: the seat before (a `Seat`). `message_reaction`: the emoji this person had on it, or null.

new.description: `my_chat_member` and `chat_member`: the seat now (a `Seat`). `message_reaction`: the emoji now, or null when they took it back.

oneOf.title: message
oneOf.description: A person wrote to the bot, or something meant for it in a group or channel: a command, a mention, a reply to one of its messages, or anything at all where the room lets the bot read every message. `replyToMessage` carries what a reply quotes when the bot was handed that too.

oneOf.title: edited_message
oneOf.description: They edited a message the bot had received, or edited one into something meant for it.

oneOf.title: comment
oneOf.description: A comment under a channel post, by the same rule as a message: a comment under the bot's own post, or answering one of its comments, counts as a reply. `message.threadRoot` is the post.

oneOf.title: edited_comment
oneOf.description: A comment the bot had received was edited.

oneOf.title: message_reaction
oneOf.description: Somebody put a reaction on a message the bot was handed (its own included), changed it, or took it back. `old` and `new` are that person's emoji, `reactions` the totals now.

oneOf.title: deleted_messages
oneOf.description: Messages were deleted for everyone. In a group: the ones the bot had received. In a private chat: any message of the chat, the bot's own included, so also the ones the bot deleted itself and a whole history the person cleared.

oneOf.title: callback_query
oneOf.description: Somebody pressed a button under one of the bot's messages. Answer it.

oneOf.title: my_chat_member
oneOf.description: The bot's own seat in a chat changed: added (with `from`, who added it), promoted, restricted, let read every message or stopped (`readsAll`), its rights moved with the group's permissions, removed, left; in a private chat, blocked (`kicked`) or unblocked (`member`). `chat` comes whole, as `GET /chats/{id}` has it but without `me`, which is `new`: right after being added a bot knows where it is and what it may do, and can say in the room why it needs to read everything, if it does.

oneOf.title: chat_member
oneOf.description: Somebody else's seat changed: joined, left, removed, banned, promoted, restricted. Only about people the bot would see on the roster: a hidden roster shows a bot that isn't an admin only the admins, a channel that hides its admins leaves them out. Sent to the bot that made the change as well.

oneOf.title: join_request
oneOf.description: Somebody asked to come in through a link that needs approval. Only to bots with the *add members* right; answer with `POST /chats/{id}/requests/{userId}`.

oneOf.title: chat_updated
oneOf.description: The room itself changed: name, description, picture, a setting, the pins, the comment switches. `chat` is the room as it is now, `changed` what moved. `from` is null in a channel that hides its admins from a bot that isn't one. The bot that made the change isn't told.

oneOf.title: web_bot_write_access
oneOf.description: Somebody said yes to the Web-Bot's `requestWriteAccess`: the private chat with them now exists (`chat`), and the bot may write first. Sent once per person.

oneOf.title: web_bot_contact
oneOf.description: Somebody shared their phone number from the Web-Bot (`requestContact`), after saying yes in the app. The number is the one verified on their account, never one typed by the page. `chat` is the private chat with them, or null when there is none yet.

Contact.description: A phone number somebody chose to share with the bot.

phone.description: E.164, as verified on their account.

key.description: The 32 raw bytes of the public key, base64url without padding.

MediaIn.description: A file to send into a readable chat, uploaded first with `POST /attachments`. What the phone needs to lay it out before downloading it.

kind.description: `audio` is a voice note; a music file is a `file` with an audio mime type.

name.description: A file name: no slashes, no control characters.

thumb.description: A tiny jpeg, base64, drawn blurred until the file is fetched.

sha256.description: Of the file as it opens; the phone checks it after downloading.

Forward.description: Who a forwarded message came from, as the forward says. The envelope is the forwarder's word: ids are only there for accounts and chats that exist.

userId.description: The person it came from, unless they switched the link to their profile off.

chat.description: The group or channel it was said in.

LinkCard.description: The card the sender's phone made for the first link in the text.

allowedReactions.description: Null or empty: any emoji. Each one at most 16 characters, as in the app.

url.description: The link to share, when the server knows its public address.

Profile.description: Somebody's public profile, as anybody in a chat with them sees it. Never a phone number.

Limits.description: Every number this server enforces on a bot, by name. A newer server may add some: read the ones you know and ignore the rest.

nameMin.description: Characters of the bot's name, at least.

usernameMin.description: Characters of a handle, at least.

usernamesMax.description: Handles in all, the main one included.

commandDescriptionMin.description: Characters of a command's description, at least.

callbackWindowMs.description: Milliseconds a press can be answered in.

webhookTimeoutMs.description: Milliseconds a webhook has to answer.

webhookMaxBackoffMs.description: Milliseconds of the longest wait between two tries of a webhook.

sendsPerSecond.description: Messages a second, all chats together.

sendsPerGroupPerMinute.description: Messages a minute into one group or channel.

sendsPerPrivatePerSecond.description: Messages a second into one private chat.

apiCallsPerMinute.description: Calls a minute, all of them.

lookupMissCost.description: What a handle nobody holds counts for, in lookups.

uploadBytesMax.description: Bytes of one file for `POST /attachments`, as this server takes them.

uploadsPerMinute.description: Uploads a minute, chat pictures included.

roomChangesPerMinute.description: Pins, reactions, room settings and room pictures a minute, in one chat.

historyLimitMax.description: Messages one page of history or comments hands back.

botsPerChat.description: Bots one group or channel can hold.
